name: media-card
description:
A card whose subject is a picture — an artifact thumbnail, a document preview, a generated image. The app has fifteen of these in a grid and the shape is doing something the plain `card` cannot: the media fills the card's whole upper area edge to edge, and the caption sits under it in a strip. A `card` pads its content; this one deliberately does not, because padding around a thumbnail wastes the only part of the card carrying information.

The placeholder is the part that gets skipped. A grid of these loads asynchronously, so most of them are empty most of the first second — and an empty card with no reserved height makes the whole grid reflow as each image lands.

base.transition: border-color var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), box-shadow var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), transform var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out)

stage.$description: A RESERVED box with an aspect ratio, not a box that grows to fit whatever arrives. A grid of these loads asynchronously and without a reserved ratio the whole grid reflows as each image lands — which is a layout shift multiplied by however many cards are on screen.

caption.$description: A strip, not a padded block. The media is the content and the caption is a label on it — giving the caption card-sized padding makes the thumbnail look like an afterthought in its own card.

title.$description: `truncate` rather than wrap. A thumbnail grid is scanned, and a two-line title in one card and a one-line title in the next makes the row's captions sit at different heights.

placeholder.$description: What fills the stage before the media arrives, and when it never does. It says the KIND in words rather than showing a broken-image glyph, because a failed thumbnail should still tell you what the thing was.

ratio.$description: The shape the stage reserves. Set it to what the source usually is — a wrong ratio still prevents the reflow, but it crops badly.

reducedMotion.$description: The lift goes; the border still warms.

a11y.note: ONE `<a>` around the whole card. The thumbnail is decorative — `alt=""` — because the title beside it is the name; an alt repeating the title makes a screen reader say it twice. Where the image IS the content and has no title, it takes a real alt instead. The kind chip is text, not colour: a file type conveyed only by a tint is a file type a colourblind user cannot read.
